parakeet: For some people in the U.S., coming out as an atheist is not just a worldview shift. It's a socioeconomic risk, a high cost one. Publicly supporting an atheist or secular organization can mean losing family support, being cut off from communal networks that have historically functioned as survival structures. It could even mean career damage, especially across the South, Midwest, and the Black and Bible Belt, being labeled dangerous, rebellious, immoral, or not raised right, and even social and relational isolation. Unlike some atheists who often lose belief, many black atheists often risk losing belief plus belonging plus basic informal safety nets. The cost feels exponentially higher. And yet secular organizations rarely account for that cost. Atheists and humanist organizations frequently say they want more diversity, but they are woefully unaware of the black tax in the U.S., ill-equipped to understand the social and economic penalties black atheists pay, and overwhelmingly uninvested in the economics required to support black secularists who are choosing to cross that line. So even when black atheists take the leap and engage with white secular spaces, they often experience double taxation. They pay the black tax for leaving their faith community in the form of loss of family, communal support, suspicion, and relational rupture. But then they also pay the secular tax, the expectation to keep up with conferences, conventions, memberships, travel, and appearances in organizations that offer none of the social or economic buffers or benefits they just lost. Most atheists lose ritual, but some atheists lose infrastructure. Most atheists lose a belief system, but some atheists often lose their support system. And the very organizations claiming to welcome them often provide no replacement, no investment, and no scaffolding. Only polite applause for representation. This is why so many remain quiet even if they agree. It's not fear of ideas, it's fear of fallout. It's fear of paying a cost no one helps them recover from. Black atheists must weigh every choice against the real risk: economic instability, broken family ties, community estrangement, and loss of cultural legitimacy. Until secular organizations understand those material realities and invest accordingly, their calls for diversity will remain hollow. Let's move into number three: assimilation survival strategy.
